title: 2. Digital Economy
subtitle: India Stack · eKYC · Digital payments · Lending · Microfinance · Crowdfunding · DigiLocker case study
subject: FinTech

sections.heading: Introduction and Learning Objectives
sections.html:
The digital economy rests on trusted identity, paperless records, instant payments and responsible credit. This module explains India Stack and its components, examines digital lending, microfinance and crowdfunding, and closes with a case study on DigiLocker.

Learning objectives

  • Explain the layers of India Stack
  • Describe Aadhaar eKYC, V-CIP and CKYC
  • Differentiate DSC and Aadhaar eSign
  • Compare digital payment modes
  • Classify digital lending models and safeguards
  • Evaluate microfinance, crowdfunding and DigiLocker

sections.heading: 2.1 India Stack
sections.html:
India Stack is a layered set of open application programming interfaces (APIs) and public digital infrastructure that allows governments, businesses and developers to deliver services that are presence-less, paperless and cashless. It is often described as a public good: instead of every bank building its own identity system and payment network, the country built shared rails on which many competing services can run.

The stack has four conceptual layers. The presence-less layer is anchored on Aadhaar, the 12-digit unique identity issued by the Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI) [1], which lets a person prove who they are remotely through biometric or one-time-password authentication. The paperless layer comprises eKYC, eSign and DigiLocker, which replace photocopies and ink signatures with verified digital records [2]. The cashless layer is the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) and related rails [3]. The consent layer, delivered through the Account Aggregator framework, allows individuals to share financial data with providers only with explicit, revocable permission [4].

1
Presence-less: Aadhaar authentication
→
2
Paperless: eKYC, eSign, DigiLocker
→
3
Cashless: UPI and payment rails
→
4
Consent: Account Aggregator

Fig. 1. The four layers of India Stack

Indian example: From account opening to credit in one afternoon

A small trader in Erode can open a bank account using Aadhaar eKYC, sign the form with Aadhaar eSign, share GST and bank data through an Account Aggregator, and receive a working-capital loan decision through a digital lender, all without visiting a branch. Each step uses a different layer of India Stack.

Design principles behind India Stack

  • Open APIs and open standards: any qualified developer or institution can build on the rails, which encourages competition.
  • Interoperability: services work across providers, so users are not locked in.
  • Digital by default and inclusive: designed for mobile phones and for people with limited documentation.
  • Consent and privacy: data moves only with the individual's permission, a principle now reinforced by data protection law [5].
  • Scale and low cost: shared infrastructure spreads fixed costs over a very large user base.

Governance of the stack

Different institutions steward different layers: UIDAI for identity, NPCI for retail payments, MeitY for DigiLocker and related public platforms, and the RBI for the regulatory framework around Account Aggregators [1], [3], [2], [4]. Independent technology volunteer groups and think-tanks contributed to design, but accountable public bodies operate the infrastructure.

Digital public infrastructure in comparison

Other countries have built comparable public digital rails. Estonia's X-Road enables secure data exchange between government and private databases, and Brazil's central bank introduced the Pix instant payment system in 2020. India's distinguishing feature is the combination of identity, payments and data-sharing layers at very large scale, which is why India Stack is studied internationally as an example of digital public infrastructure.

Key points

  • India Stack is public digital infrastructure built on open APIs
  • Layers: identity, paperless records, payments and consent
  • Competition happens on top of shared rails

sections.heading: 2.2 Unique Identification and eKYC
sections.html:
Know Your Customer (KYC) is the process by which a financial institution verifies a customer's identity and address. Traditionally this required photocopies of documents, in-person verification and manual data entry, taking days and costing banks a considerable amount per customer. eKYC digitises the process: with the customer's consent, the institution requests identity details directly from the UIDAI database, which returns verified information such as name, address, date of birth and photograph.

The Aadhaar number is issued after biometric (fingerprints and iris) and demographic data are captured. Authentication can be done by a one-time password (OTP) sent to the Aadhaar-linked mobile number, or by a biometric match. Use of Aadhaar authentication by private entities is governed by law and court rulings; only entities permitted under the Aadhaar Act and related regulations may perform it, and the customer's consent is essential [1], [6].

1

→
2
Customer gives consent
→
3

→
4

→

Fig. 2. Aadhaar eKYC process

Video-based customer identification (V-CIP) is a complementary method in which an official of the regulated entity verifies the customer through a live video interaction, with checks such as liveness, geo-tagging and a match against official records. The Central KYC (CKYC) registry, operated by CERSAI, stores a customer's KYC record once so that other regulated entities can retrieve it, avoiding repeated submission [6].

Indian example: Opening a Demat account in minutes

An investor in Madurai opens a Demat and trading account online using Aadhaar OTP, uploads a cancelled cheque photo and signs with eSign. The broker retrieves the KYC record from the registry, completes the checks and activates the account, often within the same day. The process would earlier have taken a week of paperwork.

Forms of eKYC

Table 1. Forms of electronic identity verification

FormHow it worksTypical use
OTP-based eKYCOTP sent to the Aadhaar-linked mobile numberAccount opening, SIM and wallet onboarding
Biometric eKYCFingerprint or iris matched at a deviceBusiness correspondent or branch counters
Offline verificationCustomer shares a digitally signed XML file or QR from UIDAIWhere online authentication is not required
Masked Aadhaar and Virtual IDOnly the last digits are shown, or a temporary 16-digit Virtual ID is used instead of the Aadhaar numberPrivacy-preserving verification

The Virtual ID and masked Aadhaar reduce exposure of the real Aadhaar number, which responds to privacy concerns. Even so, identity-related risks remain, such as stolen documents, SIM swaps, forged biometrics and mule accounts, so institutions combine eKYC with risk scoring, liveness detection and transaction monitoring [6].

Benefits to the system

For institutions, eKYC reduces the cost of onboarding and of document handling and lowers errors. For customers, it shortens waiting time and removes the need to travel. For the system, it improves the quality of the customer database and supports AML controls, because verified identities reduce the scope for fake accounts.

Limits and cautions

eKYC depends on correct mobile linkage and digital literacy. Customers should never share OTPs with callers, and institutions must safeguard Aadhaar data under the Aadhaar Act and data protection law [5].

sections.heading: 2.3 Digital Signature
sections.html:
A digital signature is a cryptographic technique that binds a signer to an electronic document. It provides three assurances: authenticity (the signer is who they claim to be), integrity (the document has not been altered) and non-repudiation (the signer cannot later deny signing). It works through public-key cryptography: the signer uses a private key to create a signature on a hash (a short digital fingerprint) of the document, and anyone can verify it using the matching public key.

In India the Information Technology Act, 2000 gives legal recognition to electronic records and electronic signatures [7]. Two common forms are in use. A Digital Signature Certificate (DSC) is issued by a licensed Certifying Authority after identity verification and is typically used for company filings, e-tendering and income-tax returns. Aadhaar eSign lets a person sign online by authenticating with Aadhaar; the signing key is generated for that transaction, so no physical token is required.

Table 2. DSC versus Aadhaar eSign

FeatureDigital Signature CertificateAadhaar eSign
Issued byLicensed Certifying AuthorityThrough eSign service providers using Aadhaar authentication
ValidityTypically one to three yearsSingle document or session
MediumUSB token or certificate fileNo token; online authentication
Typical usesMCA filings, e-tenders, tax returnsLoan agreements, account opening, rental agreements

How a digital signature is created and verified

  1. The signer's software computes a hash (fingerprint) of the document using an algorithm such as SHA-256.
  2. The hash is encrypted with the signer's private key, producing the digital signature, which is attached to the document.
  3. The receiver recomputes the hash of the received document.
  4. The receiver decrypts the signature using the signer's public key, available through the digital certificate.
  5. If both hashes match, the document is unaltered and was signed by the key holder.

A digital certificate binds a public key to a named person or organisation, and is itself signed by a Certifying Authority so that others can trust it. Certificates are issued at different assurance levels, and the level determines the checks made before issue and the uses permitted.

Legal framework

The Information Technology Act, 2000 provides for authentication of electronic records using digital signatures and later electronic signatures, recognises electronic records and signatures as legally valid, and establishes the regime for Certifying Authorities [7]. Certain documents, such as wills or negotiable instruments other than cheques, are excluded from this recognition; students should check the schedules of the Act.

Indian example: Signing a loan agreement from home

A borrower receives a sanction letter by email, reviews the agreement in an app and signs it using Aadhaar eSign through an OTP. The lender gets a legally valid signed PDF within minutes, reducing turnaround from days to hours.

sections.heading: 2.4 Cashless Digital Payments
sections.html:
A cashless economy depends on safe, fast and low-cost payment systems. India has built a layered system in which the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) regulates payments under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 [8], and NPCI operates retail payment systems [3].

Table 3. Major digital payment modes in India

ModeHow it worksTypical use
UPIInstant account-to-account transfers using a virtual payment address (VPA), QR code or phone number, available 24x7Everyday payments, person-to-person and merchant
IMPSImmediate interbank payment service, available at all timesQuick transfers
NEFTElectronic transfer settled in batchesRoutine transfers
RTGSReal-time gross settlement for high-value paymentsLarge business payments
AePSAadhaar-enabled payments using biometrics at a micro-ATM or business correspondentCash withdrawal and balance in rural areas
WalletsPrepaid payment instruments regulated by RBIMerchant payments and bill payments
FASTagRFID tag linked to a prepaid accountHighway toll collection
Cards and RuPayDebit and credit cards; RuPay is NPCI's domestic networkOnline and in-store purchases

Why UPI succeeded. UPI is interoperable: any UPI app can pay any bank account, so the customer is not locked into one provider. It is real-time, free or very low cost for users, and secured through two-factor authentication using the device and a PIN. Its open architecture has enabled many apps to compete on design and features while sharing the same rails [3].

Indian example: A vegetable vendor in Salem

Earlier, change shortages slowed sales and cash had to be taken to the bank. With a UPI QR code the vendor receives payments directly in a savings account and the digital trail now helps in proving income for a small business loan.

1
Small, instant: UPI
→
2
Instant, any amount: IMPS
→
3
Scheduled, routine: NEFT
→
4
Very large: RTGS

Fig. 3. Choosing a payment mode

The anatomy of a UPI payment

A UPI transaction involves a payer PSP (the app and sponsor bank on the payer's side), the NPCI switch, and the payee PSP. When a payer enters a payee's virtual address, the app sends a request that the NPCI switch resolves to the payee's bank; the payer authenticates with a PIN, the payer's bank debits the account, the payee's bank credits it, and confirmations return to both parties, usually within seconds [3].

Features and extensions of UPI

  • Collect requests and mandates: allow merchants to request payment, and customers to authorise recurring debits such as subscriptions.
  • UPI Lite and offline modes: support small-value payments with lighter authentication.
  • UPI on feature phones: services such as the *99# code and UPI 123PAY let people without smartphones make payments.
  • Credit and linked instruments: arrangements that allow certain credit lines or cards to be used through UPI.

Economics and sustainability

Government policy removed merchant discount rates on UPI transactions from 2020 to encourage adoption, which keeps costs low for merchants but raises debates on how providers can sustain investments in security and capacity. Students should follow current policy, as incentive schemes and fee rules change from time to time.

Safe payment practices

Never share a UPI PIN or OTP; verify the merchant name before paying; use only apps from official stores; and report fraud promptly through the bank and the national cyber-crime reporting portal.

sections.heading: 2.5 FinTech in the Lending Industry
sections.html:
Lending is the area where FinTech has changed credit appraisal most deeply. Traditional lenders rely on formal credit history and collateral, which excludes many first-time borrowers and small businesses. Digital lenders use alternate data, such as bank statements, GST returns, utility bill payments and mobile usage, to estimate repayment capacity, often through machine-learning models. Decisions are made in minutes, funds are disbursed digitally and repayment is collected through e-mandates or UPI.

1
Collect alternate data
→
2
Score the borrower
→
3
Instant decision
→
4
Direct disbursal
→
5
Digital repayment

Fig. 4. Digital lending journey

Types of digital lending. Peer-to-peer (P2P) platforms connect lenders and borrowers directly; in India they must be registered as NBFC-P2P and are regulated by the RBI. Marketplace lending compares offers from multiple lenders. Invoice financing, for example through TReDS platforms such as RXIL and M1xchange, lets MSMEs sell receivables from large buyers at a discount for quick cash. Buy Now Pay Later offers short-term credit at checkout, and salary advance products provide early access to earned wages.

Regulatory safeguards. Rapid growth also brought problems such as opaque pricing, harassment in recovery and misuse of data. The RBI's digital lending guidelines require, among other things, that loans be disbursed directly into the borrower's bank account, that a Key Fact Statement disclose the annual percentage rate and all charges, that lending service providers work with regulated entities, and that a grievance officer be appointed [9]. Students should refer to the latest RBI directions, as these norms are periodically updated.

Credit assessment models in digital lending

Table 4. Data sources for digital credit assessment

SourceWhat it revealsCautions
Bank statements through Account AggregatorIncome, cash flows, balancesNeeds customer consent; data quality
GST returns and invoicesBusiness turnover and seasonalityApplicable to registered businesses
Credit bureau dataPast repayment behaviourThin-file customers may have no record
Mobile and device dataStability and usage patternsPrivacy concerns; risk of bias
Utility and rent paymentsRegular payment disciplineNot always digitised

Models range from simple scorecards to machine-learning algorithms. Because decisions can be opaque, regulators emphasise transparency, fair treatment and data minimisation; lenders should be able to explain the main reasons for rejection or pricing [9].

Collections and customer protection

Repayment is increasingly collected through e-mandates and UPI autopay. Responsible lenders offer clear repayment schedules, grace for genuine hardship and respectful recovery practices. Borrowers should verify that the lender or its partner is regulated by the RBI, read the Key Fact Statement and be wary of apps that demand excessive permissions such as access to contacts and photographs.

Systemic issues

Easy credit can lead to over-indebtedness, especially among young and low-income users, and unregulated apps have harmed borrowers through abusive recovery. These experiences prompted tighter regulation and highlight that speed must be balanced with suitability.

Indian example: TReDS for a Tiruppur garment exporter

A small garment unit supplies a large retailer on 90-day credit. By uploading the invoice to a TReDS platform, the unit can get paid within days at a discount, improving working capital without borrowing against property.

sections.heading: 2.6 Microfinance and Crowdfunding
sections.html:
Microfinance is the provision of small loans, savings and insurance to low-income households that lack access to formal banks. The Grameen Bank model popularised by Muhammad Yunus used group lending and social collateral to reach poor borrowers [10]. In India, the principal channels are Self Help Groups (SHGs) of about 10 to 20 members, who pool savings and borrow from banks, and Microfinance Institutions (MFIs), many of which are NBFC-MFIs. NABARD's SHG–Bank Linkage Programme, started in the early 1990s, remains one of the world's largest microfinance initiatives. FinTech helps through digital repayments, mobile data collection and credit scoring that includes SHG behaviour.

Crowdfunding raises small amounts from a large number of contributors through an online platform. Agrawal, Catalini and Goldfarb explain that it reduces the frictions of matching entrepreneurs with dispersed funders [11]. Models differ by what the contributor receives.

Table 5. Crowdfunding models

ModelContributor receivesIndian context
Donation-basedNothing financial; goodwillMedical and social-cause fundraising on platforms such as Ketto and Milaap
Reward-basedA product or perkCreative projects and product pre-orders
Equity-basedOwnership stakeRegulatory framework in India is still evolving; investors should check current rules
Debt-based (P2P)Interest and repayment of principalRegulated through NBFC-P2P directions

Microfinance in India: structure and challenges

Microfinance is delivered through several channels: the SHG–Bank Linkage model, joint liability groups, NBFC-MFIs and small finance banks. Group lending uses peer pressure and local knowledge as substitutes for collateral, which keeps default rates low when well managed [10]. Challenges include over-lending to the same borrowers by multiple institutions, high operating costs, coercive recovery in some episodes and the risk of political interference. The crisis in one southern state around 2010 led to stronger regulation and the creation of shared credit information for microfinance borrowers.

How FinTech supports microfinance

  • Digital repayments reduce cash handling by field staff and the risk of theft.
  • Mobile data capture speeds up group meetings and record-keeping.
  • Credit bureau integration reveals multiple borrowing and prevents over-indebtedness.
  • Alternative scoring using payment histories extends credit to first-time borrowers.

The crowdfunding campaign lifecycle

1
Project idea and goal
→
2
Listing on a platform
→
3
Promotion to supporters
→
4
Funds collected and platform fee
→
5
Delivery and reporting

Fig. 5. Lifecycle of a crowdfunding campaign

Risks include fraudulent campaigns, failure to deliver promised rewards and weak investor protection in equity models. Platforms address these through verification, escrow arrangements and public updates. Regulatory treatment in India differs by model, with peer-to-peer lending regulated by the RBI while equity crowdfunding remains subject to evolving securities law [11].

Indian example: SHG with a smartphone

Women in a Nilgiris SHG record savings and loans in a mobile app and receive their bank loan repayments through UPI. The digital records form a credit history that can unlock larger loans, an example of FinTech strengthening a traditional institution.

sections.heading: 2.7 Case Study: Use of DigiLocker
sections.html:
Background. Launched in 2015 by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology as part of the Digital India programme, DigiLocker is a cloud-based platform where citizens can store and share verified documents [2]. It is a core component of the paperless layer of India Stack.

How it works. A user registers with a mobile number and links Aadhaar. Documents are of two kinds: issued documents, which agencies such as CBSE, universities, the Income Tax Department and the transport authority push directly into the user's locker, and uploaded documents, which the user scans and stores. When an employer, bank or college requests a document, the user shares a link with consent; the recipient can verify that it originates from the issuer. Under rules framed under the IT Act, issued documents in DigiLocker are treated as at par with originals [7].

Table 6. Case analysis: DigiLocker

AspectObservation
Problem solvedLost, forged or delayed paper certificates; repeated verification
StakeholdersCitizens, issuing agencies, employers, banks, universities, government
BenefitsInstant, verifiable sharing; lower paper use; faster onboarding for loans and jobs
ChallengesDigital literacy, connectivity gaps, uneven issuer coverage, privacy and consent concerns
LessonPublic digital infrastructure creates value when issuers, verifiers and users are all connected

Indian example: A student's job application

After the results are published, a university in Coimbatore pushes the mark sheet to the student's DigiLocker. When the student applies for a bank job, the recruiter verifies the certificate online without waiting for postal verification, cutting the process from weeks to a day.

An evaluation framework for DigiLocker

Table 7. Evaluating DigiLocker across four dimensions

DimensionStrengthsGaps
TechnologyCloud storage, APIs for issuers and requesters, Aadhaar-linked loginReliability and integration with legacy systems
Law and policyDocuments issued in the platform have legal validity under IT rulesAwareness among verifying bodies; evolving data protection rules
PeopleConvenient for students and workersDigital literacy and language barriers
ProcessInstant sharing and verificationUneven coverage of issuing agencies

Roles in the DigiLocker model

Issuers such as boards, universities and government departments push official documents into citizens' lockers using APIs. Requesters, including banks, employers and colleges, request documents from users with consent and verify them at source. Citizens control sharing. This three-party design removes the need to trust photocopies, because verification is at the origin [2].

Extending the model

The model can extend to land records, health records and business licences. Each new use needs consent management, grievance redress and safeguards against misuse of the same data in other settings, especially as data protection law places duties on entities that handle personal data [5].

Questions for discussion

What can be done to extend DigiLocker to people without smartphones? How should consent be designed so that sharing remains voluntary?

sections.heading: 2.8 Account Aggregator: Consent-Based Data Sharing
sections.html:
The Account Aggregator (AA) framework is a regulated mechanism by which individuals can share their financial data held with one institution (such as a bank, mutual fund or insurer) with another institution (such as a lender) in a secure, standardised and consent-driven way. Entities that perform this function are registered with the RBI as NBFC-Account Aggregators [4].

Table 8. Roles in the Account Aggregator ecosystem

RoleDescriptionExample
Financial Information Provider (FIP)Holds the customer's dataBank, mutual fund, insurer, GST network
Financial Information User (FIU)Requests and uses the data to offer a serviceLender, wealth platform
Account AggregatorNeutral intermediary that manages consent and routes data without reading itLicensed NBFC-AA
CustomerGives, reviews and revokes consentIndividual or business
1
Customer receives request from lender
→
2
Customer approves consent in AA app
→
3
AA sends consent to data provider
→
4
Data provider shares encrypted data
→
5
Lender gets data and decides

Fig. 6. Data flow through an Account Aggregator

Key features. A consent artifact records what data, for what purpose and for how long; the AA is data-blind, meaning it passes encrypted data without viewing it; consent can be revoked at any time. Benefits. Borrowers avoid paper statements; lenders get reliable data for cash-flow-based lending; and individuals gain control over how their financial data is used. Limitations. Adoption depends on the number of providers and users on the network, on digital literacy and on clear explanations of consent so that people understand what they approve.

Indian example: Loan for a small shop

A kirana shop owner consents to share bank statements and GST data via an Account Aggregator. A lender evaluates cash flows, offers a working-capital line within a day and does not require the owner to gather paper statements.

Discussion

How can consent screens be designed so that people genuinely understand what they approve rather than clicking through?

sections.heading: Chapter Summary
sections.html:
Chapter summary

  • India Stack provides presence-less, paperless, cashless and consent layers on open APIs
  • eKYC and eSign reduce onboarding time from days to minutes
  • UPI succeeded through interoperability, low cost and real-time settlement
  • Digital lending uses alternate data but needs strong consumer safeguards
  • DigiLocker demonstrates the value and limits of public digital infrastructure

sections.heading: Review Questions
sections.html:
The questions follow the revised Bloom's taxonomy (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyse, Evaluate, Create); the level is shown in italics after each question. Answer each in your own words, using the module and the Indian examples.

Short answer questions

  1. State the four layers of India Stack. (Remember)
  2. Define eKYC and video-based customer identification (V-CIP). (Remember)
  3. List any four digital payment modes in India and state one feature of each. (Remember)
  4. Explain how a digital signature provides authenticity, integrity and non-repudiation. (Understand)
  5. Distinguish between a Digital Signature Certificate and Aadhaar eSign. (Understand)
  6. Explain how TReDS helps micro, small and medium enterprises manage working capital. (Understand)
  7. Explain the role of an Account Aggregator in consent-based data sharing. (Understand)
  8. A borrower with no formal credit history applies for a loan through a mobile app. Identify the data sources a digital lender may use and the safeguards the borrower should expect. (Apply)
  9. A Self Help Group wants to digitise its savings and loan records. Suggest suitable FinTech tools and explain the expected benefits. (Apply)
  10. Show how DigiLocker can speed up the job application of a fresh graduate applying to a bank. (Apply)

Long answer questions

  1. Explain India Stack with reference to its layers, design principles and governance, giving Indian examples. (Understand)
  2. Describe the Aadhaar eKYC process step by step, discuss its benefits and limitations, and illustrate with the opening of a Demat account. (Apply)
  3. Compare UPI, IMPS, NEFT, RTGS and AePS, explain why UPI has succeeded and analyse the concerns about its sustainability. (Analyse)
  4. Analyse how FinTech has changed lending, covering credit assessment, types of digital lending, RBI safeguards and the risk of over-indebtedness. (Analyse)
  5. Evaluate microfinance and crowdfunding as tools of financial inclusion. Which is more suitable for rural entrepreneurs in India? Justify your view. (Evaluate)
  6. Evaluate DigiLocker using the dimensions of technology, law, people and process, and propose improvements to extend its benefits to people without smartphones. (Create)

sections.heading: Glossary
sections.html:
TermMeaning
India StackA layered set of open APIs and public digital infrastructure for identity, paperless records, payments and consent.
AadhaarA 12-digit unique identity number issued by UIDAI on the basis of biometric and demographic data.
eKYCElectronic Know Your Customer verification using an authenticated digital identity with the customer's consent.
V-CIPVideo-based Customer Identification Process, a live video verification by an official of a regulated entity.
CKYCThe Central KYC registry that stores a customer's KYC record for use by other regulated entities.
Virtual IDA temporary 16-digit number that can be used instead of the Aadhaar number to protect privacy.
Digital signatureA cryptographic technique that binds a signer to an electronic document.
DSCDigital Signature Certificate issued by a licensed Certifying Authority.
eSignAadhaar-authenticated online signing of documents.
UPIUnified Payments Interface, a real-time, interoperable account-to-account payment system.
VPAVirtual Payment Address used to receive UPI payments without sharing account details.
NEFT / RTGS / IMPSInterbank transfer systems: batch-settled, real-time gross settlement for large values, and immediate transfers.
AePSAadhaar-enabled Payment System using Aadhaar and biometrics at micro-ATMs.
NBFC-P2PA non-banking finance company registered to operate a peer-to-peer lending platform.
TReDSTrade Receivables Discounting System, a platform where MSME invoices are financed.
Key Fact StatementA standardised disclosure of the cost and key terms of a loan.
SHGSelf Help Group, a small group of members who pool savings and borrow collectively.
CrowdfundingRaising small amounts from many contributors through an online platform.
Account AggregatorA regulated intermediary that manages consent and routes financial data between providers and users.
DigiLockerA government cloud platform for storing and sharing verified digital documents.
